chapters.subtitle: From the grower’s phone to the grower’s reward
intro: This page follows one capture through the Greenstand system. A capture is one photo of a tree, with its GPS point and some data. A grower takes it with the Treetracker app.
Chapter 1 follows the capture from the grower’s phone to the grower’s reward. This page says "grower". Older code and tables say "planter" for the same person.

stages.title: On the phone: the grower takes a capture
story: The grower opens the Treetracker app on an Android phone. On the first day, the grower signs up with a name, a phone number or an email, and a selfie. On later days, the grower picks a name from a list on the phone.

The grower walks to a young tree and taps TRACK. The app waits until the GPS point is stable. The grower takes a photo of the tree, checks it, and can add a note. The app keeps the photo and the GPS point on the phone, so the grower needs no network.

stages.title: The upload: from the phone to cloud storage
story: Later, in a place with internet, the grower taps UPLOAD. The app sends each photo to cloud storage. Then it sends a small data file, a "bundle". A bundle lists up to 50 captures: where, when, and which photo.
The app then marks each capture as uploaded and deletes the photo from the phone.

stages.title: The bundle chain: four small services open the bundle
story: Cloud storage tells a small Greenstand service that a new bundle arrives. That service keeps the bundle. Every 5 minutes, a second service opens the new bundles. A third service passes each capture on to the service that stores it. A fourth service, the older path, also gets each capture. It stores the older tree record itself, if that record is not there yet.
These four services are public Greenstand repos. They are not in the docs repo yet, so they have no viewer.

stages.title: Verification: an admin checks the photo
story: An admin signs in to the admin panel and opens the Verify page. The page shows a grid of photos that wait for verification. The admin looks at each photo.

The admin approves the photo, with the type of planting, the age of the tree, and the species if the admin knows it. Or the admin rejects it, with a reason, for example "Not a tree" or "Blurry photo". On the web map, an approved capture shows "Verified". A rejected capture is not active any more, so the map hides it.

stages.title: The reward: the grower earns money
story: In the code, one organization has a payment rule. An automatic job counts the approved captures of each of its growers. It pays in steps of 100 captures: 100 captures give 120,000 leones, and 1,000 captures or more give the maximum, 1,200,000 leones. The job writes an "earning" with the status "calculated".

Greenstand’s guide to earnings and payments gives the next steps for a typical case. In that case, a funder does them. A funder is the person or the organization that pays for the captures. The funder opens the Earnings page of the admin panel and downloads the list. Then the funder pays each grower outside the Greenstand system. Last, the funder logs the payments. The funder logs one earning in its detail panel, or many earnings with a file upload on the Payments page. Each logged earning becomes "paid". The guide says that the growers can see the payment data. But the Treetracker app and the wallet app have no earnings screen. So the grower learns about the money from the payment itself.

flags.text: The organization is FCC, which we think is Freetown City Council. The job and the payments still run today. (The code shows no change since 2023.)
flags.question: Is FCC the Freetown City Council, does the FCC earnings job still run, and do the funders still pay the growers and log the payments this way?

flags.text: The wallet app tells each new user "we will gift you 1 token". The token does not arrive today.

stages.note: Tokens are not a grower reward today. An operator can start a job that puts one token for each approved capture of an organization’s growers into a wallet that the operator names. Greenstand’s white paper describes a goal, not the code of today. In that goal, each capture becomes a token in the wallet of the entity that is responsible for the tree. When claims conflict, the grower comes first. The token also holds a proof of the payment to the grower. The token job of today does not use the wallet of the grower, and no token holds payment data.

chapters.subtitle: The capture on the public web map
intro: This chapter follows one capture onto the public web map, map.treetracker.org. Anyone can open the map and see the trees that growers captured.
The web map shows a capture in two ways. Close up, it is a pin. From further away, it is a part of the number on a cluster. A click on a pin opens the tree page.

stages.title: The pin: the capture is on the map before verification
story: When the field data service stores the capture (chapter 1, stage 4), the database also keeps an older tree record of it. This record is "active" at once. It is not "approved" yet.

The map is a set of small square images, the tiles. The browser asks the tile server for each tile. The mark "active" shows a capture on the map. So close up, the new capture is a pin at once, before an admin verifies it.
stages.note: Greenstand’s product page says that the web map shows verified trees. Today, the map shows each active capture, also before verification.

stages.title: The clusters: a job adds the capture to the counts
story: From further away, the map groups the captures into round clusters. A cluster shows a number: the count of its captures.

An automatic job is set to run every 2 hours. It finds the active captures that are not in a cluster yet. Then it builds the clusters again. Until the next run, the new capture is a pin close up. It is not in the counts yet.

stages.title: The approval: only the tree page changes
story: An admin approves the capture (chapter 1, stage 5). The admin panel saves "approved" in the record. It also saves the age of the tree, the type of planting, and the species if the admin knows it. Nothing sends a message to the map. The pin and the counts stay the same.
Only the tree page changes. Its badge "Waiting for verification" becomes "Verified". If the admin rejects the capture, the record is not active any more. Then the map hides it.

story: A visitor clicks a pin. The web map opens the tree page beside the map. The page shows the photo, the tree number, the badges, the date of the capture, the country, and the species. The photo comes straight from cloud storage.
The web map keeps each tree page for a time before it builds the page again. So "Verified" can show hours after the approval.

chapters.subtitle: The capture as an impact token
intro: This chapter follows one capture to an impact token. An impact token is a record in a wallet. It points to one capture. It is not money: it has no price, and it does not pay the grower.
Greenstand’s white paper and its model pages describe a goal for tokens. This chapter shows the code of today. A note at a stage says where the goal and the code differ.

stages.title: The approval: no token yet
story: An admin approves the capture (chapter 1, stage 5). The older tree record has a field for a token, but the field stays empty. Nothing makes a token at this step. An open issue in Greenstand’s wallet code asks for a token at the approval.

So the screens say that no token exists. In the admin panel, the capture detail says "Impact token not issued", and a filter of the Captures page shows "Not Tokenized". On the web map, the tree page shows the badge "Token not issued".

images.alt: A drawing of the two screens after the approval, with made-up data: the admin panel shows Capture #1234 as "Approved" with "Impact token not issued", and the web map shows Tree #1234 as "Verified" with "Token not issued"
images.caption: A drawing of an approved capture with no token

stages.title: The mint: an operator makes the tokens
story: Later, a Greenstand operator starts a job by hand. No timer starts it. The operator names an organization and a wallet. The job finds each approved capture of the growers of that organization that has no token yet.

For each of these captures, the job makes one impact token in the named wallet. A token is a small record: it points to one capture and to one wallet. A capture can have only one token. The operator picks the wallet, not the grower.

flags.text: An operator still starts this job today. The wallet is usually the wallet of the organization.
flags.question: Does an operator still run the create_tokens job, when was the last run, for which organizations, and who picks the wallet?

stages.note: Greenstand’s white paper describes a goal. In that goal, a capture holds its first wallet, and the grower comes first. The system makes a token only when no other claim conflicts. Today, the field data service stores a target wallet with each session of the app, but the token job does not read it.

stages.title: Transfers: the holder sends tokens to other wallets
story: The holder of a wallet can send tokens to another wallet, for example the wallet of a funder. If the holder controls both wallets, or the two wallets trust each other, the tokens move at once. Otherwise, the other side must accept the transfer first. The wallet service records each move of a token.

An organization uses the wallet admin panel to send a number of tokens. A person can use the newer wallet app. It shows the tokens, accepts transfers, and makes share links with a QR code. Anyone who opens a share link can claim its tokens into a new wallet. A transfer can also mark tokens as "claimed". A claimed token cannot move again.

flags.text: The wallet admin panel and the wallet app both work in production today. They use two versions of the wallet service that share one set of wallets.
flags.question: Which versions of treetracker-wallet-api run in production today, and which one does the wallet admin panel use?

stages.note: The white paper describes five token states and trade on a blockchain. The code has no blockchain. It marks a token only as "in a transfer" or "claimed". A claimed token is the nearest to a retired token of the white paper.

stages.title: The token page: anyone can see the token
story: On the web map, the badge of the tree page now says "Token issued". The token page shows the token number, the date, the tree, and the wallet that holds the token. It also shows the claim status, and if the token can move. A timeline shows each transfer between wallets. The wallet app links to the same page.
A wallet page shows the name of the wallet and how many tokens it holds. No page shows a price. A token holds no money and no payment data.
stages.note: Greenstand’s product page says that investors and consumers can buy, sell, and trade impact tokens, and that this pays the grower. The white paper gives each token a value. The business model on Greenstand’s model page names an impact token fee of 3% of the uploaded captures. The code of today has none of these. A token has no price and no value, and it moves only by transfer. The token job takes no fee, and a token does not pay the grower.

chapters.subtitle: The capture in the data for organizations
intro: This chapter follows one capture into the data that an organization gets. A grower works with an organization, for example a group that plants trees. The captures of the grower belong to that organization.
Greenstand sends no report to an organization. A person of the organization signs in to the admin panel to see the data. One organization gets cards with more numbers.

stages.title: The account: a person of the organization signs in
story: A Greenstand maintainer gives a person of the organization an account in the admin panel. The role of the account names the organization.
When the person signs in, the admin panel asks only for the data of that organization. So the person sees the captures and the growers of that organization.

stages.title: The export: the person downloads a spreadsheet
story: On the Captures page, the person sees the captures of the organization. By default, the list shows the captures that no admin approved yet and the captures that an admin approved. A filter can make the list smaller.
The button “Export Captures” opens a dialog. The person picks the columns, and the admin panel downloads a spreadsheet file with one row for each capture. The file holds up to 20,000 captures.
stages.note: Greenstand’s product page says that the web map and the admin panel show the trees on a map. An organization can then confirm the place and the health of each tree. The admin panel of today shows the data in a list, in numbers, and in a file. The public web map shows the trees on a map.

stages.title: The Home page: four numbers
story: The Home page of the admin panel shows four numbers for the organization. They are “Total Captures”, “Untagged Captures” (the captures that no admin approved yet), “Verified Captures”, and “Growers”.
The numbers count the captures and the growers that the admin panel asks for (stage 1). When an admin approves a capture, the capture moves from “Untagged Captures” to “Verified Captures”.
stages.note: Greenstand does not send these numbers to the organization: no report, no email, and no message. A person must sign in to see them. The impact tokens of the organization are in its wallet.
